items.text: EVE separates a visual display from four directional buttons; cursor control differs from direct touchscreen selection.
Shaping, success tones and reinforcement establish effective actions before the animal enters more demanding games.
Cursor navigation, identity matching, delayed matching and reversal learning test different requirements.
The published advancement study retained engagement and improved familiar-task performance after games introduced unrewarded errors.
Response trajectories and rated personality profiles differ among sea lions and must be considered alongside task history.
Gameplay metrics, offered-diet consumption and clinical records describe different outcomes and require separate interpretation.

slides.title: Two buttons can generate diagonal cursor movement
body: EVE offered four directional buttons, but a sea lion could contact two at once. Simultaneous contacts combined two movement directions. Upward and rightward input produced a diagonal route. The gameplay study classified this as **diagonal movement**. The response therefore depended on the overlap between contacts, adding a way to move across the display beyond separate horizontal and vertical steps.

Diagonal input differed from staircasing in its temporal organization. Staircasing alternated contact with horizontal and vertical buttons. Its route contained successive steps in different directions. Diagonal movement used both directions during the same period. The computer and video records distinguished these response sequences, retaining how the animal coordinated its button contacts while moving the cursor toward a displayed goal.

Both sequences used directional assignments established during earlier training. A sea lion could combine or alternate those acquired responses. Their effects depended on when the buttons were engaged. Strategy coding preserved that organization within successful cursor trials. The available controller therefore supported several routes to a target, linking the timing of individual contacts to the geometry of movement generated on the screen.

slides.title: Circling repeats a cycle of directional inputs
body: The gameplay analysis defined **circling** as a cycle of directional presses. Five inputs occurred in clockwise or counterclockwise order. A sequence could proceed upward, rightward, downward, leftward and upward again. Those inputs returned movement to an earlier direction. The coded strategy identified a recurring organization of familiar responses, tracing how button order shaped a route rather than treating every press as an isolated event.

Circling differed from direct targeting even though both used the same buttons. Targeting moved toward the goal with one or two useful inputs. Circling cycled through directional assignments in a repeated order. The study restricted its definition to movement within less than half the screen. This spatial criterion separated a local cycle from longer routes involving travel around the display's boundaries.

The computer recorded the contacts that generated each movement. Video coding identified their organization as a strategy episode. Repeated directional cycles could therefore be followed within a larger trial. Their duration and press counts entered the movement analysis. These records connected the sea lion's sequence of physical responses with the cursor's changing route.

slides.title: An initial movement can precede target-directed control
body: The study also coded a category called **superstitious movement**. It consisted of an initial directional input followed by a pause. Only the first movement of the trial qualified for this category. The label referred to an observed response pattern. Its definition kept an early contact separate from later movements that carried the cursor toward the current target.

The cursor's initial movement changed its position before the pause. The sea lion could then provide a different directional input. The ensuing route continued from that changed location. Target contact still determined whether the trial succeeded. The sequence therefore joined an opening response with later control, retaining the distinction between the first action and the movements that completed the goal-directed portion of the trial.

Operational coding classified actions by their order and timing. It placed the early movement in a defined category when the pause criterion was met. Later targeting or other strategies could occur in the same trial. The resulting record retained several episodes within one completed attempt. This approach linked the animal's response history to its current movement sequence.

slides.title: Game sessions reinforce voluntary blood sampling
body: Winship and colleagues describe EVE use after important husbandry behaviors. **Husbandry** includes routine care and trained cooperation with health procedures. One application followed **venipuncture**, the collection of blood through a vein. The sea lion completed the trained sampling behavior first. Access to the game then provided an additional consequence, linking participation in veterinary care with an activity the animal repeatedly chose to perform.

One sea lion had not provided a voluntary blood draw during its annual examination for four years. After EVE entered its regular enrichment plan, it provided samples twice a year. Trainers offered game interaction immediately after the completed behavior. The described sequence connected successful sampling with access to computerized enrichment. The paper reports this as a husbandry application within the animal's care history.

The game retained its own response and reinforcement opportunities after access was provided. The sea lion could operate the controller and complete cursor trials. Those consequences occurred within the activity following the blood draw. Care staff thereby linked two trained interactions in sequence. Completion of the health behavior preceded access to EVE, joining voluntary cooperation with later opportunities for active control of the computerized task.

slides.title: Game variety is rotated within ordinary care sessions
body: EVE was incorporated into the existing care program rather than supplied as an additional daily session schedule. Its session lengths resembled other in-pen training activities. It could also form a shorter component of an open-water session. The number of daily sessions was retained. Computerized enrichment therefore became another activity within the established rotation.

After the sea lions mastered cursor training, the games offered varied across sessions. Different games changed the response problem while preserving the acquired controller skills. Staff used this rotation to add cognitive challenge. It also addressed **habituation**, reduced responding after repeated exposure to a familiar event. The program combined varied gameplay with other standard forms of enrichment.

Changing the game altered what the animal needed to accomplish with the controller. Cursor movement remained available through its directional buttons. A maze required an appropriate route, while matching required a sample-related choice. The sea lion could carry established motor responses into these different problems. Session rotation therefore varied the consequences of those responses.

slides.title: Personnel ratings use extended observation of each animal
body: Ramos and Winship obtained personality ratings from trainers familiar with each sea lion. Eligible personnel had at least **six months** of direct experience with the animal. They rated recurring traits using a common survey. Each trait used a **five-point scale**. The ratings therefore drew on extended observation in managed care, linking a shared descriptive instrument to the different behavioral histories personnel had encountered with individual animals.

Multiple trainers supplied ratings for the same sea lion. Their observations could include different sessions and care interactions. The study examined consistency among those ratings. Related traits were then organized into broader clusters. This sequence retained both the individual animal and the shared trait descriptions, connecting repeated personnel observations with a structured profile that could be compared with computerized gameplay measurements from the same participant.

The rated animals had already completed the EVE cursor-training sequence. Their profiles were related to latency and button use in computerized sessions. These measures supplied task-specific records alongside broader observations from care. A shared rating instrument connected those two kinds of information. Personnel observed recurring behavior over a longer period than the individual trials measured within a game.

slides.title: Goats acquire an ordered two-step food-box response
body: Briefer and colleagues trained goats to obtain food from a transparent box. The first action pulled a lever outward using a rope. The second lifted that lever with the mouth or muzzle. Lifting released food into a bowl. This **two-step task** required the actions in an effective order, linking manipulation of the apparatus to a consequence available only after the appropriate physical sequence was completed.

Training began with the final action already made accessible. The lever was extended before the goat lifted it. Later trials required pulling and lifting in sequence. This procedure is **shaping**, reinforcing progressively closer forms of the required behavior. It established the food-releasing action before adding the preceding movement, giving the animal experience with the endpoint that the full sequence eventually had to reach.

Successful goats acquired the sequence within **8–22 training trials**. They used their lips, teeth or muzzle to operate the device. The completed movements released food through the apparatus rather than through a computer-controlled cursor. The resulting behavior joined two acquired actions into one effective sequence. Ordered input therefore governed access to reward in a physical task.

slides.title: A learned manipulation persists after months without use
body: The goat study tested memory after the two-step task had been acquired. The box became unavailable between testing periods. Goats then encountered the same pull-and-lift requirement again. The first memory test followed **26–33 days** of retention. A later test followed **281–311 days** after the first, extending the time during which the acquired physical sequence had to remain available without continued practice on the apparatus.

All tested successful goats completed the sequence within one trial when it was offered again. Their first memory-test solutions averaged approximately **21.9 s**. Solutions in the later test averaged approximately **38.8 s**. These latencies recorded execution after extended absence from the task. The animals retained the ordered actions that released food, connecting their original training history with renewed operation of the same box months later.

The learning phase had linked pulling the lever with subsequently lifting it. Both actions remained necessary when the apparatus returned. The goats produced that sequence after the long intervals. Food release supplied the same consequence upon completion. The retained response joined memory for an acquired manipulation with renewed access to reinforcement, extending the relationship between ordered action and outcome beyond the period of regular training.

slides.title: Chimpanzees use tools to move food through a shared maze
body: Padrell and colleagues offered sanctuary-housed chimpanzees a physical food maze. The device measured approximately **1 × 0.5 m**. Transparent panels enclosed shelves with openings at their ends. Animals used sticks or branches to move food toward those openings. The task required manipulating a reward through a visible route, linking tool movement to eventual extraction from the apparatus rather than to a cursor event on a screen.

The maze was double-sided, with an opaque divider separating its two faces. Two animals could therefore work at different sides simultaneously. Food was distributed across the shelves rather than placed only at the top. The chimpanzees encountered rewards at several route positions. This design supplied multiple opportunities for tool contact and extraction within one shared enrichment device.

All chimpanzees contacted the device, although participation varied substantially among individuals. Africa and Coco learned to retrieve rewards reliably. Other animals used tools without completing the full extraction route. The study followed both contact and successful task execution. These outcomes retained the distinction between exploring an interface and mastering the movements that obtain its reward.

slides.title: Food-maze participation changes across repeated sessions
body: The chimpanzee study compared loaded-maze days with days when the same maze was empty. Observations followed task participation and other behavior. Loaded days provided visible food distributed across the shelves. Empty days retained the physical apparatus without those rewards. The comparison therefore followed use of a familiar device under different feeding opportunities, linking participation to the current availability of food within a shared social environment.

Participation was higher in the morning than in the afternoon. It also declined across repeated sessions. Individual involvement ranged from very brief contact to more than half of observation scans. **Scan sampling** records behavior at designated observation moments. These records preserved variation across animals and times of day, following how sustained access to the same enrichment problem interacted with its changing use over successive opportunities.

Task participation accompanied increased tool use and reduced inactivity. The chimpanzees spent more time acting on the device while engaging with its food routes. The observations also recorded changes in social and self-directed behavior. Greater involvement therefore occurred within the animals' broader daily activity. The study connected manipulation of the shared maze with shifts in what participants did around it.

slides.title: Relational matching compares relations rather than icons
body: Truppa and colleagues tested **relational matching-to-sample** in capuchin monkeys. A sample array contained either repeated or different icons. Comparison arrays also expressed same or different relations. The correct choice matched the sample's relationship. The individual icons could differ between sample and comparison, requiring selection based on how elements related within each array rather than a physically identical picture shared across the two arrays.

The monkey first touched the sample on a touchscreen. Two comparison arrays then appeared below it. Touching the comparison with the matching relation produced a food pellet. An incorrect selection produced a timeout without that reward. This response sequence joined inspection of the sample array with a direct-contact choice, linking the relation among visible elements to a consequence delivered by the computerized apparatus.

Initial training used arrays with two icons, while later conditions varied the array size. Increasing the number of elements changed the available information about repetition or difference. Particular icon identities changed across stimulus sets. The relationship within each array remained the required basis for matching. The preparation extended conditional choice from identity between objects to similarity between relations.

slides.title: Capuchin relational transfer survives changes in array size
body: Roberta acquired relational matching after extensive experience with arrays of icons. Truppa and colleagues then changed the materials used to express the relations. Tests included new icons and inverted familiar icons. Other tests changed the number of elements. These manipulations preserved same or different as the required match while altering the visible features through which each relationship appeared within the sample and comparison arrays.

Transfer performance was approximately **67.7% correct** with two-icon arrays. It was approximately **66.7%** with sixteen-icon arrays. The available sample still specified the relation to select. Each comparison contained its own arrangement of elements. Correct responses extended the acquired relationship beyond the four-icon training format, linking prior touchscreen experience to judgments made with substantially smaller and larger visual arrays during the new tests.

Physical identity between individual icons was not required across sample and comparison. The useful correspondence concerned sameness or difference within each array. Roberta retained that response requirement across changes in appearance and element count. Selection of the matching relation continued to produce reinforcement. The transfer joined an acquired comparison of relations with new visual formats.

refs: Leach PT, Hayes J, Pride M, Silverman JL, Crawley JN (2016). Normal Performance of Fmr1 Mice on a Touchscreen Delayed Nonmatching to Position Working Memory Task. eNeuro 3(1):ENEURO.0143-15.2016. https://doi.org/10.1523/ENEURO.0143-15.2016
slides.title: Touchscreen memory guides selection of a new position
body: Leach and colleagues trained mice in **nonmatching to position**. A sample appeared at one touchscreen location. A later choice rewarded the other location. The correct response therefore differed from the position contacted earlier. This rule linked memory of a preceding spatial response to a new selection, extending direct-contact computer testing from choosing a visible stimulus to using prior trial information to determine where to act.

The delayed version inserted **1, 3 or 10 s** between sample and choice. Longer delays increased the interval over which the location had to remain available. Accuracy declined with increasing delay. The same nonmatch rule remained in place throughout. Changing the waiting period therefore altered the retention demand while keeping the response relation and reward condition shared across the three timed versions of the task.

The study compared mice lacking functional **Fmr1** with wild-type mice carrying the usual gene. Fmr1 encodes fragile X mental retardation protein, or **FMRP**. Both groups acquired the nonmatch response and showed comparable performance in this preparation. Their choices tracked the remembered location and the intervening delay. The results connected a defined genetic comparison with task-specific memory behavior.

refs: Castro L, Nowak R, Dufour V (2026). Smart Ungulates: What Sheep and Goats' Performances in a Reversed-Reward Contingency Task Tell Us About the Evolution of Cognitive Flexibility. Ecology and Evolution 16:e72506. https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.72506
slides.title: Choosing less food can earn the larger reward
body: Castro and colleagues tested a **reversed-reward contingency** in goats and sheep. Two visible food quantities were offered as alternatives. Selecting the smaller quantity delivered the larger reward. Selecting the larger quantity delivered the smaller reward. The animal therefore had to choose according to the consequence of its selection, replacing a direct approach to the most food with a response that gained more food through the task's rule.

**Inhibitory control** means suppressing a strongly favored response when another action is required. Here, approaching the larger visible quantity competed with the rewarded selection. Successful behavior required choosing the smaller alternative instead. The study also followed adjustment across corrective procedures. These procedures changed the experience supplied by the task while preserving the central distinction between the quantity selected and the quantity received after that selection.

Two young goats reached criterion without corrective procedures. Two more succeeded after those procedures were introduced. Sheep remained at or below chance-level performance in the tested task. The individual outcomes linked the reversed contingency with different learning trajectories. Successful goats redirected selection according to the later reward, connecting inhibition of the immediate larger-food response with adjustment to the consequences of choosing among familiar visible alternatives.
